```{r setup}
res_dir <- file.path("..", "outputs", "results")
load_res <- function(name) readRDS(file.path(res_dir, paste0(name, ".rds")))
m0 <- load_res("m0")
m1 <- load_res("m1")
m2 <- load_res("m2")
m3 <- load_res("m3")
m4 <- load_res("m4")
m5 <- load_res("m5")
m6 <- load_res("m6")
m7 <- load_res("m7")
hl <- load_res("headline")

# Typst can only read files under the report folder, so figures are copied next to it.
fig_dir <- "_fig"
dir.create(fig_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
fig <- function(name) {
  src <- file.path("..", "outputs", "figures", name)
  dst <- file.path(fig_dir, name)
  file.copy(src, dst, overwrite = TRUE)
  knitr::include_graphics(dst)
}
pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
num <- function(x, d = 3) formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f", big.mark = ",")
int <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
pval <- function(p) ifelse(p < 1e-4, "< 0.0001", sprintf("%.4f", p))
tbl <- function(df, ...) knitr::kable(df, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, ...)
ci <- function(row) {
  sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", num(hl$metrics[row, "estimate"]), num(hl$metrics[row, "lower"]),
          num(hl$metrics[row, "upper"]))
}
n_class <- colSums(m0$class_source)
```

# Abstract

PhishScope asks how far classical probability and statistics can go in separating phishing
emails from legitimate mail. Using `r int(m0$rows_kept)` deduplicated emails from six public
corpora, we extract 18 transparent features and apply Modules 1 to 7 of the course. A naive
Bayes model built only from features that pass a Holm-corrected chi-square test with
Cramer's V of at least 0.1 (PhishScore) reaches sensitivity `r ci("sensitivity")`, specificity
`r ci("specificity")` and AUC `r num(hl$auc)` on a held-out test set (Wilson 95% intervals).
At a realistic 1% phishing prevalence, precision falls to `r num(hl$precision_1pct_deployed)`,
and sensitivity on an unseen corpus drops by `r num(hl$sensitivity_drop)`, so the score is an
early-warning aid, not a filter.

# Problem

Phishing emails try to steal credentials or money by imitating trusted senders. Most filters
are opaque machine learning models. This project asks a narrower question: which simple,
countable signals differ between phishing and legitimate mail, how strong are those
differences, and how reliable would a transparent rule-based score be in practice?

# Data

The data is the Kaggle Phishing Email Dataset (Al-Subaiey et al. 2024), which bundles six
corpora. The combined file was skipped because it duplicates the per-source files. Classes:
legitimate is label 0; phishing is label 1 from Nazario or Nigerian Fraud; every other label 1
email is spam. Of `r int(m0$rows_loaded)` rows, `r int(m0$dropped[["empty_body"]])` with empty
bodies and `r int(m0$dropped[["duplicate"]])` duplicates (same lowercase subject and body after
collapsing whitespace) were removed. A 70/30 split stratified by class and source gives the
train and test sets; all analysis below uses the training set unless stated.

```{r data-table}
cs <- as.data.frame.matrix(m0$class_source)
cs <- data.frame(source = rownames(cs), cs, check.names = FALSE)
tbl(cs, caption = "Emails by source and class after cleaning")
```

Totals: `r int(n_class[["legitimate"]])` legitimate, `r int(n_class[["phishing"]])` phishing
and `r int(n_class[["spam"]])` spam. Phishing comes from only two sources, so source and class
are partly confounded, and Enron and Ling are entirely lowercase.

# Feature extraction

Each email becomes 18 numbers computed from subject and body with plain ASCII regular
expressions, so the same code runs in R and in the browser. Lexicon counts (urgency,
credential, money words, generic greetings) use whole-word matching against a fixed list in
`config/features.yml`. URL features count links and flag bare IP hosts, shorteners and `@`
inside links. Style features are exclamation marks, the uppercase share of letters, body
length, word count, HTML tags and runs of all-caps words in the subject.

# Module 1: Descriptive statistics

```{r m1}
s <- m1$stats[, c("feature", "class", "mean", "median", "sd", "cv", "skewness")]
s[, 3:7] <- lapply(s[, 3:7], signif, 3)
tbl(s, caption = "Location, spread and shape by class (training set)")
```

```{r m1-fig, fig.cap = "Body length by class (log1p scale)"}
fig("m1_box_body_chars.png")
```

All four features are strongly right-skewed in every class, so medians describe them better
than means. Phishing emails are longer (median `r int(s$median[s$feature == "body_chars" & s$class == "phishing"])`
characters) and use more capitals than legitimate mail. Spam is shortest and uses the most
exclamation marks.

# Module 2: Random variables and Bayes

```{r m2}
b <- m2$bayes[, c("feature", "p_f_phish", "p_f_not_phish", "post_sample", "post_1pct")]
b[, 2:5] <- lapply(b[, 2:5], round, 4)
names(b) <- c("feature", "P(f | phish)", "P(f | not phish)", "P(phish | f), sample",
              "P(phish | f), 1%")
tbl(b, caption = "Conditional probabilities and Bayes posteriors")
```

```{r m2-fig, fig.cap = "PMF of n_urls by class (10+ pooled)"}
fig("m2_pmf_n_urls.png")
```

A generic greeting raises the chance of phishing from `r pct(m2$prior_sample)` to
`r pct(b[[4]][b$feature == "generic_greeting"])` in the sample, but only to
`r pct(b[[5]][b$feature == "generic_greeting"])` at 1% prevalence. Worked example:
`r m2$worked[["one_pct"]]`. The number of URLs has variance far above its mean, and the
moments recovered from the numerical MGF derivatives match the direct ones.

# Module 3: Correlation and regression

```{r m3}
lc <- m3$lpm_coef
lc[, -1] <- lapply(lc[, -1], signif, 3)
tbl(lc, caption = "Linear probability model (phishing vs legitimate) with logistic comparison")
```

```{r m3-fig, fig.cap = "Spearman correlation of each feature with phishing"}
fig("m3_rho_is_phish.png")
```

Credential and money words have the strongest rank correlation with phishing. The
rank-difference formula gives `r num(as.numeric(m3$rank_formula[["formula"]]), 5)` against
`r num(as.numeric(m3$rank_formula[["cor"]]), 5)` from `cor()`. The linear probability model
explains R squared = `r num(m3$r_squared)` (multiple R `r num(m3$multiple_r)`), but
`r pct(m3$out_of_range)` of its fitted values fall outside [0, 1], which is why the logistic
fit is shown beside it.

# Module 4: Probability distributions

```{r m4}
f4 <- m4$fits
f4$aic <- round(f4$aic, 1)
f4$bic <- round(f4$bic, 1)
tbl(f4[, c("class", "distribution", "aic", "bic", "winner")],
    caption = "Gamma, Weibull and lognormal fits to body length (thousands of characters)")
```

```{r m4-fig, fig.cap = "n_urls observed vs Poisson"}
fig("m4_poisson_n_urls.png")
```

The lognormal wins on both AIC and BIC in every class. The Poisson model fails for link counts
(dispersion index up to `r num(max(m4$poisson$dispersion_index), 0)`), and log body length is
not normal (Shapiro p < 0.0001). Simulated batches of 50 emails follow the binomial closely,
and Nazario inter-arrival times in the densest year fit an exponential with rate
`r num(m4$exponential$rate_per_day)` per day (KS p = `r num(m4$exponential$ks$p.value)`).

# Module 5: Large-sample tests

```{r m5}
t5 <- m5$tests[, c("name", "statistic", "critical", "p_value", "decision", "effect_name",
                   "effect")]
t5$statistic <- round(t5$statistic, 2)
t5$p_value <- pval(t5$p_value)
t5$effect <- round(t5$effect, 3)
tbl(t5, caption = "Z tests, alpha = 0.05")
```

```{r m5-fig, fig.cap = "Effect sizes of the phishing vs legitimate Z tests"}
fig("m5_effect_sizes.png")
```

With thousands of emails per class almost every test rejects, so effect sizes carry the
message: credential words, generic greetings and urgency words have large effects, while
exclamation marks differ only trivially. `r m5$error_note`

# Module 6: Small samples, chi-square and ANOVA

```{r m6}
ind <- m6$independence[, c("feature", "chi2", "cramers_v", "odds_ratio", "or_low", "or_high",
                           "p_holm", "passes")]
ind$chi2 <- round(ind$chi2, 1)
ind[, 3:6] <- lapply(ind[, 3:6], signif, 3)
ind$p_holm <- pval(ind$p_holm)
tbl(ind, caption = "Binary feature x class independence, ranked by Cramer's V")
```

```{r m6-fig, fig.cap = "One-way ANOVA residuals, QQ plot"}
fig("m6_anova_residual_qq.png")
```

Six features pass Holm p < 0.05 with V of at least 0.1 and feed PhishScore. With n = 20 per
class, the Welch t test detected the body length difference in only
`r pct(m6$small_rejection_rate[["welch"]], 0)` of 500 draws. One-way ANOVA on log body length
rejects equal means (partial eta squared `r num(m6$anova$effect[1])`); Levene rejects equal
variances, so the F test is approximate. `r m6$doe_note`

# Module 7: Reliability

```{r m7}
sr <- m7$system_rates
sr[, -1] <- lapply(sr[, -1], signif, 3)
tbl(sr, caption = "Rules as components: independence prediction vs observed (test set)")
```

```{r m7-fig, fig.cap = "Probability that a user sees no missed phish"}
fig("m7_user_reliability.png")
```

Treating each rule as a component, independence overstates the chance that any rule fires,
because rules tend to fire together. For a user whose mail is 1% phishing, a missed phish
arrives about every `r int(round(m7$user_level[["mttf_emails"]]))` emails, or every
`r num(m7$user_level[["mttf_days"]], 1)` days at 50 emails a day. Under an assumed 90-day
refresh with 2 degraded days, availability is `r num(m7$availability[["availability"]])`.

# PhishScore validation

```{r validation}
mt <- data.frame(metric = rownames(hl$metrics), estimate = num(hl$metrics[, "estimate"]),
                 lower = num(hl$metrics[, "lower"]), upper = num(hl$metrics[, "upper"]))
tbl(mt, caption = "Test set, threshold 0.5, Wilson 95% intervals")
cc <- hl$cross_corpus
cc[, -1] <- lapply(cc[, -1], round, 3)
tbl(cc, caption = "Nigerian Fraud vs test legitimate, with and without Nigerian Fraud in training")
```

```{r roc-fig, fig.cap = "ROC curve on the test set"}
fig("m7_roc.png")
```

PhishScore uses `r length(hl$features)` binary features with Laplace-smoothed likelihoods and
a training prior of `r pct(hl$prior)`. On the test set it reaches AUC `r num(hl$auc)`. At 1%
prevalence the same operating point gives precision `r num(hl$precision_1pct_deployed)`;
re-scoring with a 1% prior raises it to `r num(hl$precision_1pct_prior)` at the cost of
sensitivity. Trained without Nigerian Fraud, sensitivity on that corpus falls from
`r num(cc$sensitivity[1])` to `r num(cc$sensitivity[2])`.

# Web demo

A static page (`web/`) runs the same feature extraction and PhishScore in the browser from
`web/model.json`. It shows the score at the dataset prior and at a 1% prior, a red-flag table
with likelihood ratios and the matched words. Nothing is sent to a server, and a parity test
checks that the JavaScript features and scores match R to six decimals.

*Screenshot placeholder: web demo with the suspicious example.*

# Limitations

- **Corpus age and confounding.** Several corpora are decades old, and phishing comes from
  only two sources, so some features partly identify the source rather than the class.
- **Lexicon features.** A fixed English word list misses paraphrases, other languages and
  image-based phishing, and attackers can avoid it once it is known.
- **Naive Bayes independence.** Rules are positively dependent, so the model double-counts
  correlated evidence and its probabilities are overconfident.
- **Observational DOE.** The block and Latin square layouts arrange existing emails; nothing
  was randomly assigned.
- **Association, not causation.** Every result describes how features co-occur with labels in
  this dataset, not why emails are phishing.

# Conclusion

A handful of countable signals, mainly credential words, generic greetings, money words and
urgency, separate phishing from legitimate mail with large effect sizes, and a transparent
naive Bayes score built from them reaches an AUC of `r num(hl$auc)`. The base rate dominates
in practice: at 1% prevalence most alerts are false alarms, and performance drops on an unseen
corpus. PhishScope is best used as an explainable early-warning aid.
